en.tip: Commutation is fundamentally a current-transfer/turn-off process.

en.stem: Choose correct option about the Smart Building Energy Automation (SBEA). Statement-1: It is based on development of complete building energy management system excluding battery management system. Statement-2: It manages and controls multiple-connected battery packs. It monitors the battery quantities SOC–SOH–DOD.
options: Statement-1 is False, but Statement-2 is True
Statement-1 is True, but Statement-2 is False
en.quick: Smart Building Energy Automation integrates monitoring, control, communication and optimization of building loads and may coordinate local generation and storage. The first statement excludes battery management from a complete energy-management system and is therefore not a correct description; the second statement is consistent with smart-building automation. The resulting combination is option A.
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
Smart Building Energy Automation integrates monitoring, control, communication and optimization of building loads and may coordinate local generation and storage. The first statement excludes battery management from a complete energy-management system and is therefore not a correct description; the second statement is consistent with smart-building automation. The resulting combination is option A.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**SBEA integrates loads, controls, sensors and often distributed energy/storage**

### Exam Takeaway
A “complete” smart-building energy system is integrated, not artificially isolated from storage.

### Common Mistake
Do not assume battery/storage coordination is outside modern building energy management.

### Quick Trick
A “complete” smart-building energy system is integrated, not artificially isolated from storage.
en.tip: A “complete” smart-building energy system is integrated, not artificially isolated from storage.

en.stem: A room is 120 feet by 60 feet with 16 feet ceiling. A luminaire is suspended 4 feet below the ceiling and the work plane is 4 feet above the floor. The value of room cavity ratio (RCR) is
en.quick: The luminaire is 4 ft below a 16-ft ceiling and the work plane is 4 ft above the floor, so cavity height is 8 ft. Room cavity ratio is RCR=5h(L+W)/(LW). Substituting h=8 ft, L=120 ft and W=60 ft gives RCR=1.0, matching option B.
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
The luminaire is 4 ft below a 16-ft ceiling and the work plane is 4 ft above the floor, so cavity height is 8 ft. Room cavity ratio is RCR=5h(L+W)/(LW). Substituting h=8 ft, L=120 ft and W=60 ft gives RCR=1.0, matching option B.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**RCR=5h(L+W)/(LW)=5×8×180/(120×60)=1.0**

### Exam Takeaway
Use the vertical distance from luminaire plane to work plane as cavity height.

### Common Mistake
Do not use the full ceiling height as h when luminaires are suspended and a work plane is specified.

### Quick Trick
Use the vertical distance from luminaire plane to work plane as cavity height.
en.tip: Use the vertical distance from luminaire plane to work plane as cavity height.

en.stem: Choose the correct option. Statement-1: In parallel MTDC system, the valve-voltage rating is related to the power rating. Statement-2: In series MTDC system, the valve-current rating is related to the power rating.
options: Statement-1 is True, but Statement-2 is False.
Statement-1 is False, but Statement-2 is True.
en.quick: In a parallel MTDC system all terminals operate at essentially the same DC voltage, so power rating is mainly reflected in current rating rather than valve-voltage rating. In a series MTDC system the same current flows through all terminals, so individual terminal power is mainly reflected in its voltage contribution rather than valve-current rating. Thus both printed statements are false, giving option D.
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
In a parallel MTDC system all terminals operate at essentially the same DC voltage, so power rating is mainly reflected in current rating rather than valve-voltage rating. In a series MTDC system the same current flows through all terminals, so individual terminal power is mainly reflected in its voltage contribution rather than valve-current rating. Thus both printed statements are false, giving option D.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**Parallel MTDC: common Vdc, variable Id**

**Series MTDC: common Id, variable Vdc**

### Exam Takeaway
Parallel → common voltage; series → common current.

### Common Mistake
Do not relate the common quantity to terminal power rating; the varying quantity carries the power difference.

### Quick Trick
Parallel → common voltage; series → common current.
en.tip: Parallel → common voltage; series → common current.

en.stem: The power flow control strategy that is typically used in Series MTDC systems is
options: to control a constant voltage at all converter stations.
to set current by one of the converter stations and is kept common for all the converter stations.
to control power flow depending on load.
to control power flow depending on frequency.
en.quick: Because all terminals in a series MTDC link carry the same DC current, the natural coordinated strategy is to control a common current and regulate each terminal power through its DC voltage. The strategy described in option B is therefore used for series MTDC operation.
formula: Pi=Vi Id with common Id in a series MTDC link
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
Because all terminals in a series MTDC link carry the same DC current, the natural coordinated strategy is to control a common current and regulate each terminal power through its DC voltage. The strategy described in option B is therefore used for series MTDC operation.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**Pi=Vi Id with common Id in a series MTDC link**

### Exam Takeaway
Series MTDC: one common current, terminal voltage sets terminal power.

### Common Mistake
Do not apply the parallel-MTDC common-voltage control concept to a series link.

### Quick Trick
Series MTDC: one common current, terminal voltage sets terminal power.
en.tip: Series MTDC: one common current, terminal voltage sets terminal power.

en.stem: Choose the correct option. Statement-1: Voltage instability is more severe at the voltage setting terminal (VST) compared to other terminals irrespective of whether it is rectifier or inverter in HVDC system. Statement-2: Constant AC voltage control at VST improves voltage stability at all terminal including VST without any coordination.
options: Statement-1 is True, but Statement-2 is False
Statement-1 is False, but Statement-2 is True
en.quick: Voltage instability in an MTDC/HVDC network is strongly influenced by which terminal regulates DC voltage and by whether that terminal is operating as rectifier or inverter; it is not universally “more severe at the VST irrespective of mode.” The correct truth combination in the source is option B.
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
Voltage instability in an MTDC/HVDC network is strongly influenced by which terminal regulates DC voltage and by whether that terminal is operating as rectifier or inverter; it is not universally “more severe at the VST irrespective of mode.” The correct truth combination in the source is option B.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**DC-network voltage stability depends on converter control mode and network operating point**

### Exam Takeaway
Statements containing “irrespective of rectifier/inverter operation” deserve careful scrutiny.

### Common Mistake
Do not generalize voltage-stability behavior without considering converter operating mode and control characteristic.

### Quick Trick
Statements containing “irrespective of rectifier/inverter operation” deserve careful scrutiny.
en.tip: Statements containing “irrespective of rectifier/inverter operation” deserve careful scrutiny.

en.stem: As per National Building Code (NBC 2016) the Refuge Area is defined as an area within the building for
options: a temporary use during egress and generally serves a staging area which is protected from the effect of fire and smoke.
a storage space for firefighting equipment located on every floor.
an open terrace used for emergency helicopter rescues.
a basement area designated for evacuation during earthquakes.
en.quick: NBC 2016 defines a refuge area as a designated safe area within a high-rise building where occupants can temporarily assemble or wait during an emergency before rescue or further evacuation. It is a life-safety provision, which is the description given by option A.
formula: Refuge area = temporary safe holding area during emergency evacuation/rescue
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
NBC 2016 defines a refuge area as a designated safe area within a high-rise building where occupants can temporarily assemble or wait during an emergency before rescue or further evacuation. It is a life-safety provision, which is the description given by option A.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**Refuge area = temporary safe holding area during emergency evacuation/rescue**

### Exam Takeaway
Refuge area is for emergency life safety, not normal occupancy.

### Common Mistake
Do not treat a refuge area as an ordinary recreation or service space.

### Quick Trick
Refuge area is for emergency life safety, not normal occupancy.
en.tip: Refuge area is for emergency life safety, not normal occupancy.

en.stem: A piece of wood is described by z = 0, 30° < ϕ < 60°. Given the following statementsStatement 1:The piece of wood includes neither the x-axis nor the y-axisStatement 2:The piece of wood is infinitely longChoose the correct option for the above statements
options: Statement 1 is true, but statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false, but statement 2 is true
Both statements 1 and 2 both are true
en.quick: The surface z=0 with 30°<φ<60° is a sector-shaped region of the xy-plane between two rays. Because neither φ=0° nor φ=90° is included, it contains neither the positive x-axis nor positive y-axis, while the radial extent is not bounded by the angular condition. The statement combination is option D.
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
The surface z=0 with 30°<φ<60° is a sector-shaped region of the xy-plane between two rays. Because neither φ=0° nor φ=90° is included, it contains neither the positive x-axis nor positive y-axis, while the radial extent is not bounded by the angular condition. The statement combination is option D.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**z=0**

**30°<φ<60°**

### Exam Takeaway
Read cylindrical-coordinate inequalities geometrically: z fixes a plane and φ fixes angular rays.

### Common Mistake
Do not invent a radial boundary when no limit on ρ is given.

### Quick Trick
Read cylindrical-coordinate inequalities geometrically: z fixes a plane and φ fixes angular rays.
en.tip: Read cylindrical-coordinate inequalities geometrically: z fixes a plane and φ fixes angular rays.

en.stem: When we say that the electrostatic field is conservative, we do not mean that
options: The work done in a closed path inside the field is zero
The potential difference between any two points is zero
It is the gradient of a scalar potential
en.quick: A conservative electrostatic field has zero closed-loop line integral, path-independent potential difference and zero curl in a simply connected electrostatic region. Conservativeness does not mean the electric field has zero divergence everywhere, because divergence is related to charge density. The statement in option C is therefore the one we do not mean.
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
A conservative electrostatic field has zero closed-loop line integral, path-independent potential difference and zero curl in a simply connected electrostatic region. Conservativeness does not mean the electric field has zero divergence everywhere, because divergence is related to charge density. The statement in option C is therefore the one we do not mean.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**∮E·dl=0**

**∇×E=0**

**∇·D=ρv**

### Exam Takeaway
Conservative relates to curl/path independence, not necessarily divergence.

### Common Mistake
Do not infer “no sources” from “conservative.” Charges can exist in an electrostatic field.

### Quick Trick
Conservative relates to curl/path independence, not necessarily divergence.
en.tip: Conservative relates to curl/path independence, not necessarily divergence.

en.stem:
Given the following statements:
Statement 1:A periodic signal cannot be anticausal.
Statement 2:An energy signal must be of finite duration.
Choose the correct option for the above statements
options: Statement 1 is true, but statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false, but statement 2 is true
en.quick: A nonzero periodic signal repeats indefinitely; if it were zero for all positive time as a purely anticausal signal, periodic repetition would force it to be zero everywhere. An energy signal, however, need not have finite duration—for example an exponentially decaying signal can extend indefinitely yet have finite energy. Hence statement 1 is true and statement 2 false: option A.
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
A nonzero periodic signal repeats indefinitely; if it were zero for all positive time as a purely anticausal signal, periodic repetition would force it to be zero everywhere. An energy signal, however, need not have finite duration—for example an exponentially decaying signal can extend indefinitely yet have finite energy. Hence statement 1 is true and statement 2 false: option A.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**Energy E=∫|x(t)|²dt <∞**

### Exam Takeaway
Finite energy does not imply finite duration.

### Common Mistake
Do not confuse time support with convergence of the energy integral.

### Quick Trick
Finite energy does not imply finite duration.
en.tip: Finite energy does not imply finite duration.

en.stem:
For a static magnetic field, the following statements are givenStatement 1:It is solenoidal.
Statement 2:It is conservative.
Choose the correct option for the above statements
options: Statement 1 is true, but statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false, but statement 2 is true
en.quick: Magnetic flux density is solenoidal because ∇·B=0—there are no magnetic monopoles. A static magnetic field is not generally conservative in regions containing current, since Ampère’s law gives ∇×H=J. Therefore statement 1 is true and statement 2 is false, matching option A.
en.detailed:
### Statement-wise Analysis
**Statement 1: True**

**Statement 2: False**

### Concept and Reasoning
Magnetic flux density is solenoidal because ∇·B=0—there are no magnetic monopoles. A static magnetic field is not generally conservative in regions containing current, since Ampère’s law gives ∇×H=J. Therefore statement 1 is true and statement 2 is false, matching option A.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**∇·B=0**

**∇×H=J**

### Exam Takeaway
Magnetic B is always divergence-free; H may have curl where current exists.

### Common Mistake
Do not apply the electrostatic condition ∇×E=0 directly to magnetostatic H in a current-carrying region.

### Quick Trick
Magnetic B is always divergence-free; H may have curl where current exists.
en.tip: Magnetic B is always divergence-free; H may have curl where current exists.

en.stem: Consider following statements: Assertion: DC series motors are suitable for electric locomotives. Reason: DC series motors provide high starting torque. Of these statements:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
en.quick: A DC series motor develops very high starting torque because, before saturation, flux is approximately proportional to armature current and torque T∝ΦIa≈Ia². This makes it suitable for traction applications such as electric locomotives. Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion: option A.
formula: T∝ΦIa; unsaturated series motor Φ∝Ia → T∝Ia²
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
A DC series motor develops very high starting torque because, before saturation, flux is approximately proportional to armature current and torque T∝ΦIa≈Ia². This makes it suitable for traction applications such as electric locomotives. Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion: option A.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**T∝ΦIa**

**unsaturated series motor Φ∝Ia → T∝Ia²**

### Exam Takeaway
Series motor + traction → remember high starting torque.

### Common Mistake
Do not operate a DC series motor at no load because its speed can rise dangerously.

### Quick Trick
Series motor + traction → remember high starting torque.
en.tip: Series motor + traction → remember high starting torque.

en.stem: Out of the following systems with input x(t) and output y(t), identify the linear system.
en.quick: A system is linear when input, output and output derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together; coefficients may still depend on time. In option B, dy/dt+2t y=t²x satisfies this condition. The other listed equations contain squared signal terms. Therefore option B is linear.
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
A system is linear when input, output and output derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together; coefficients may still depend on time. In option B, dy/dt+2t y=t²x satisfies this condition. The other listed equations contain squared signal terms. Therefore option B is linear.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**Linear form: a1(t)dy/dt+a0(t)y=b0(t)x**

### Exam Takeaway
Time-varying coefficients do not make a system nonlinear.

### Common Mistake
Look for powers/products of x, y or derivatives, not merely the presence of t-dependent coefficients.

### Quick Trick
Time-varying coefficients do not make a system nonlinear.
en.tip: Time-varying coefficients do not make a system nonlinear.

en.stem: Consider the following statements: Assertion: Single-phase induction motor is not self-starting. Reason: Net rotating magnetic field produced by single-phase winding at standstill is zero. Of these statements:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.
en.quick: At standstill a single-phase stator field can be resolved into equal forward and backward rotating fields. Their starting torques are equal and opposite, giving zero net starting torque; hence the motor is not self-starting. Both assertion and reason are true and the reason correctly explains the assertion: option A.
formula: At standstill: Tf=Tb in opposite directions → Tnet=0
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
At standstill a single-phase stator field can be resolved into equal forward and backward rotating fields. Their starting torques are equal and opposite, giving zero net starting torque; hence the motor is not self-starting. Both assertion and reason are true and the reason correctly explains the assertion: option A.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**At standstill: Tf=Tb in opposite directions → Tnet=0**

### Exam Takeaway
Single-phase induction motor needs an auxiliary starting means because forward/backward torques cancel at rest.

### Common Mistake
After the rotor starts, the two slips differ and the torques no longer cancel.

### Quick Trick
Single-phase induction motor needs an auxiliary starting means because forward/backward torques cancel at rest.
en.tip: Single-phase induction motor needs an auxiliary starting means because forward/backward torques cancel at rest.

en.stem: Consider the following statements: Assertion: The no-load current of an induction motor is usually more than that of a transformer of similar rating. Reason: An induction motor can be considered as a generalized transformer. Of these statements:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.
en.quick: An induction motor requires appreciable magnetizing current because its magnetic circuit includes an air gap, whose reluctance is much larger than the nearly closed iron path of a transformer. Hence its no-load current is generally higher. Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason statement as printed is not the complete/correct explanation expected by the item, leading to option B.
formula: Large air-gap reluctance → higher magnetizing mmf/current
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
An induction motor requires appreciable magnetizing current because its magnetic circuit includes an air gap, whose reluctance is much larger than the nearly closed iron path of a transformer. Hence its no-load current is generally higher. Both assertion and reason are true, but the reason statement as printed is not the complete/correct explanation expected by the item, leading to option B.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**Large air-gap reluctance → higher magnetizing mmf/current**

### Exam Takeaway
Induction motor no-load current is high mainly because of its air gap.

### Common Mistake
When evaluating assertion–reason items, require the reason to explain the assertion directly, not merely be a true related statement.

### Quick Trick
Induction motor no-load current is high mainly because of its air gap.
en.tip: Induction motor no-load current is high mainly because of its air gap.

en.stem: Consider following statements: Assertion: When a line-to-line (L-L) fault takes place at the terminals of an open-circuited generator, the phase voltages are sometimes indeterminate though line voltages are always determinable. Reason: During L-L fault, a zero-sequence voltage is always indeterminate. Of these statements:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true, but Reason is false.
Assertion is false, but Reason is true.
en.quick: For an L-L fault there is no zero-sequence current, so the zero-sequence network is not fixed by current flow. At open-circuited generator terminals this can leave the common zero-sequence voltage reference indeterminate even though line-to-line voltages remain uniquely determined. Hence both assertion and reason are true and the reason explains the assertion: option A.
formula: L-L fault: I0=0; line voltages are independent of common zero-sequence voltage shift
en.detailed:
### Concept and Reasoning
For an L-L fault there is no zero-sequence current, so the zero-sequence network is not fixed by current flow. At open-circuited generator terminals this can leave the common zero-sequence voltage reference indeterminate even though line-to-line voltages remain uniquely determined. Hence both assertion and reason are true and the reason explains the assertion: option A.

### Calculation / Key Relation
**L-L fault: I0=0**

**line voltages are independent of common zero-sequence voltage shift**

### Exam Takeaway
A common phase-voltage shift cancels in line-to-line voltages.

### Common Mistake
Do not infer that indeterminate phase reference makes line voltage indeterminate.

### Quick Trick
A common phase-voltage shift cancels in line-to-line voltages.
en.tip: A common phase-voltage shift cancels in line-to-line voltages.

en.stem: In a transfer function representation of a system, what does the denominator polynomial represent?
en.quick: D — Characteristics of the system. The denominator gives the characteristic equation; its roots determine the poles and natural response of the represented system.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: D — Characteristics of the system**

### Denominator and characteristic equation
A **transfer function**  relates the Laplace transform of the output to that of the input for a linear time-invariant system with zero initial conditions. It is written as a ratio of two polynomials:

G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) = N(s)/D(s)

Characteristic equation: D(s) = 0

The roots of the denominator are the **system poles** , after any common numerator–denominator factors have been cancelled. These poles describe the modes that appear in the natural response. Their positions determine whether a response decays, grows or oscillates, and how quickly the transient dies out. This is why the denominator represents the system’s characteristics.

### How the denominator describes the response
For example, consider G(s) = 5/(s² + 3s + 2). Factor the denominator and set it equal to zero:

s² + 3s + 2 = (s + 1)(s + 2) = 0

Poles: s = −1 and s = −2

The corresponding natural-response terms are proportional to e^−t and e^−2t. Both decay, so these modes are stable; the pole at −1 produces the slower decay. The numerator controls the zeros and gain of this transfer function. A reduced transfer function may hide cancelled internal modes, so transfer-function poles alone do not always describe every internal state.

### Quick Trick
Denominator → D(s)=0 → poles → stability.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A is the external excitation, not a denominator property. B is the response variable, not the denominator polynomial. C is too narrow: a denominator may contain several dynamic parameters, not one ‘frequency constant’. D correctly captures the characteristic dynamics.

### Common Mistake
Treating the entire denominator polynomial as a single time or frequency constant instead of recognizing it as the characteristic polynomial.
en.tip: Denominator → poles; numerator → zeros. That two-word association solves many control-system MCQs.

en.stem: The steel strands in ACSR conductors are typically made up of ______
en.quick: A — Galvanized for corrosion resistance. In conventional ACSR, zinc-coated steel strands provide mechanical reinforcement and resist corrosion.
formula: KEY RELATION / LOGIC: ACSR = Aluminium conductor strands + high-strength galvanized steel core.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: A — Galvanized for corrosion resistance**

### Construction of an ACSR conductor
**ACSR**  means **Aluminium Conductor Steel Reinforced** . It consists of aluminium strands arranged around a steel core. Aluminium provides high conductivity with relatively low weight and carries most of the line current. The steel core provides tensile strength, allowing the conductor to withstand tension, wind loading and the mechanical demands of long spans.

In conventional ACSR construction, the steel strands are **galvanized** , meaning they are coated with zinc. The coating separates the steel from moisture and air, reducing rust formation. Zinc also provides sacrificial protection: where a small coating defect exposes steel, the zinc preferentially corrodes and helps protect the steel underneath.

Corrosion protection matters because rust reduces the effective steel cross-section and weakens the conductor’s mechanical support. Thus, the treatment named in the answer preserves the strength and service life of the steel core. It is not primarily intended to increase electrical conductivity. Special aluminium-clad steel-core conductors exist, but the question asks about the typical galvanized-steel ACSR construction.

### Quick Trick
ACSR: Al conducts, Steel reinforces, Zinc protects.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
B wrongly assigns the steel core a conductivity-driven purpose. C tinning is not the standard ACSR steel-core treatment. D annealing would reduce hardness/strength and is not the defining protective treatment.

### Common Mistake
Thinking every conductor component is optimized mainly for conductivity; ACSR deliberately separates electrical and mechanical functions.
en.tip: If an ACSR question asks ‘why steel?’, answer strength; if it asks ‘why galvanized?’, answer corrosion resistance.

subject: Electrical Engineering
concept: Maximum Earth Resistance for Large Power Stations

en.stem: What is the maximum permissible earth resistance for large power stations?
en.quick: C — 0.5 Ω. This is the large-power-station earth-resistance value expected in the supplied examination.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: C — 0.5 Ω**

### Earth resistance and fault-current discharge
The expected maximum earth resistance for a **large power station is 0.5 Ω** . The earthing grid connects equipment frames, structures and other bonded metalwork to a common network of buried conductors and electrodes. It provides a path for earth-fault current and helps control dangerous potential differences during a fault.

When current enters the soil through the grid, the grid potential rises relative to remote earth. For a simplified resistive model, this rise is:

Earth-potential rise ≈ I_gR_g

Here I_g is the current actually discharged from the grid into earth, and R_g is the grid resistance. For the same discharged current, a lower grid resistance produces a smaller potential rise. Large stations can experience substantial fault currents, which explains the low resistance value used in this question.

The 0.5 Ω figure is the answer to this examination item. In an actual earthing design, resistance alone does not establish safety: grid geometry, soil resistivity, current division, fault-clearing time, and permissible touch and step voltages must also be considered. A low measured resistance and safe surface-potential gradients are related but distinct requirements.

### Quick Trick
Large power station → very low resistance → 0.5 Ω.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
8 Ω, 5 Ω and 2 Ω are too high for the conventional large-power-station value used in such MCQs. The keyed value is 0.5 Ω.

### Common Mistake
Memorizing one earth-resistance value for every installation type; permissible targets differ by application and standard.
en.tip: In earthing MCQs, larger fault level generally means a stricter (lower) target earth resistance.

en.stem: What does TCR stand for in the context of power systems?
en.quick: C — Thyristor-Controlled Reactor. A TCR varies the inductive current drawn by a shunt reactor by controlling the thyristor firing angle.
formula: Reactor current is controlled by thyristor firing angle α
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: C — Thyristor-Controlled Reactor**

### TCR construction and operation
A **Thyristor-Controlled Reactor (TCR)**  contains an inductor connected in series with two thyristors in antiparallel. One thyristor conducts during one current half-cycle and the other conducts during the opposite half-cycle. Changing their firing angle changes the interval for which reactor current flows, thereby controlling its fundamental-frequency component.

With the firing-angle reference convention normally used for a TCR, α = 90° gives full reactor conduction. Increasing α towards 180° reduces conduction, and at 180° the reactor is effectively blocked. The reactor therefore behaves as a controllable inductive shunt element.

### Role in reactive-power compensation
A TCR **absorbs inductive reactive power** . In a Static Var Compensator, it is commonly combined with capacitor branches. The capacitor branches provide capacitive VARs, while the TCR adjusts inductive VAR absorption so that the complete compensator can regulate bus voltage and reactive-power exchange.

The word **reactor**  identifies the inductive element; **thyristor-controlled**  identifies how its current is varied. Phase-angle control produces harmonics at intermediate conduction angles, so practical installations use suitable connections and filtering.

### Quick Trick
R in TCR literally stands for Reactor.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A, B and D are non-standard expansions in this context. C is the established power-system abbreviation.

### Common Mistake
Confusing TCR with a rectifier because thyristors are used. The controlled element is a reactor branch, not a DC rectifier output.
en.tip: TCR = reactor + thyristor firing-angle control; TSC = capacitor + thyristor switching.

en.stem: Ward leonard method of speed control is used because of:
options: Fine speed control over whole range
high overall efficiency of the system
en.quick: A — Fine speed control over whole range. The Ward Leonard system provides smooth DC motor speed variation by adjusting the generator output voltage.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: A — Fine speed control over whole range**

### How the Ward Leonard system controls speed
In the **Ward Leonard system** , a prime mover drives a DC generator, and the generator supplies the armature of the DC motor being controlled. Adjusting the generator field current changes its generated voltage. This provides a continuously adjustable armature voltage for the controlled motor.

N ∝ (V_a − I_aR_a)/Φ

Here V_a is motor armature voltage, I_aR_a is the armature resistance drop, and Φ is motor field flux. With approximately constant motor flux, increasing the generator output voltage increases motor speed. Reducing the voltage reduces speed smoothly, including operation at low speeds.

Below base speed, armature-voltage control normally gives a constant-torque operating region within current limits. Above base speed, weakening the motor field can extend the speed range, approximately at constant power. Reversing generator voltage reverses motor direction, and suitable arrangements also permit electrical braking.

The main benefit is therefore **fine, smooth speed control over a wide range** . The motor–generator set requires several machines, space and maintenance, and introduces additional conversion losses. Its historical appeal was controllability, particularly for duties such as hoists and rolling mills.

### Quick Trick
Ward–Leonard’s headline advantage: stepless control.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
B is not the defining advantage. C is false because the equipment is costly. D is false because multiple rotating-machine conversions reduce overall efficiency compared with modern electronic drives.

### Common Mistake
Choosing ‘high efficiency’ because the control is smooth. Smoothness and efficiency are different; the classic set has substantial conversion losses.
en.tip: Ward–Leonard = variable generator voltage applied to DC motor armature.

en.stem: Which type of generator does not require a separate power source for excitation and operates at variable speeds?
en.quick: D — Induction generator. It generates when driven above synchronous speed and needs no separate DC rotor-excitation supply, although magnetizing reactive power is still required.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: D — Induction generator**

### How an induction machine generates
An **induction generator**  is an induction machine driven mechanically in its generating region. For a conventional grid-connected machine, generation occurs when the rotor turns faster than the rotating stator field. Its slip becomes negative:

N_s = 120f/P

s = (N_s − N_r)/N_s

N_r > N_s gives s < 0

Here f is supply frequency, P is the number of poles, N_s is synchronous speed and N_r is rotor speed in rpm. In this region, electromagnetic torque opposes the mechanical drive. Mechanical power supplied by the prime mover is converted into electrical power delivered through the stator.

### What “no separate excitation source” means
The rotor does not need the separate DC field supply used by a conventional wound-field synchronous generator. However, the air-gap magnetic field still requires **magnetizing reactive power** . A grid-connected induction generator draws it from the grid or local compensation. A suitable standalone self-excited arrangement obtains it from capacitors, subject to residual magnetism, speed and load conditions.

A directly grid-connected induction generator operates over a limited speed range above synchronous speed while grid frequency remains fixed. A wide variable-speed range generally requires power-electronic conversion. Thus, the answer does not mean that excitation energy is unnecessary or that every induction generator supports unrestricted speed variation.

### Quick Trick
Induction machine above synchronous speed → generator.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A requires separate field excitation. B is identified as a motor, not the requested generator. C normally needs rotor field excitation. D best matches the stated characteristics.

### Common Mistake
Saying an induction generator is completely self-excited in every case. Grid-connected units take magnetizing VARs from the grid; isolated units need suitable capacitors and residual magnetism.
en.tip: Induction generator: no separate DC field system, but still needs magnetizing reactive power.

en.stem: Swing equation of synchronous machine:
options: describe the rotor dynamics of synchronous machine
is a linear second order differential equation
analyse the friction and windage loss
en.quick: A — It describes the rotor dynamics of a synchronous machine. The swing equation relates the mechanical–electrical power imbalance to rotor-angle acceleration.
formula: Pe = Pmax sin δ in the classical lossless model
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: A — describe the rotor dynamics of synchronous machine**

### Power imbalance and rotor motion
A synchronous machine stores kinetic energy in its rotating mass. At steady operation, mechanical input and electrical output are balanced after losses are accounted for. A disturbance changes this balance, causing the rotor to accelerate or decelerate relative to the synchronously rotating reference.

For the classical model with damping neglected and powers expressed per unit on a consistent machine base, the **swing equation**  is:

(2H/ω_s) d²δ/dt² = P_m − P_e

H is the inertia constant in seconds, ω_s is synchronous electrical angular speed, δ is rotor electrical angle relative to the synchronous reference, and P_m − P_e is accelerating power. Positive accelerating power speeds up the rotor; negative accelerating power slows it down.

### Connection to stability
In a simple generator–infinite-bus model, electrical output takes the form P_e = P_max sin δ. Substitution makes the swing equation a **nonlinear second-order differential equation** . Solving it shows how rotor angle changes after a disturbance and whether the machine remains in synchronism.

A linear equation can be obtained for small deviations around an operating point, but that is an approximation. The general equation describes rotor dynamics and is central to transient-stability analysis.

### Quick Trick
‘Swing’ means the rotor swings relative to the synchronous field.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
B is incorrect because the electrical-power term is generally nonlinear in δ. C concerns mechanical losses, not the main purpose of the swing equation. D is too narrow and wrongly says it ‘determines’ steady-state stability; the equation describes rotor dynamics, especially transient behaviour.

### Common Mistake
Calling the swing equation a linear second-order equation without stating a small-signal linearization assumption.
en.tip: Swing equation = accelerating power → rotor-angle acceleration.

en.stem: In galvanizing, the metal surface is coated with a layer of ______
en.quick: C — Zinc. Galvanizing protects iron or steel with a zinc coating that acts as a barrier and provides sacrificial corrosion protection.
formula: KEY RULE: Galvanizing = coating iron/steel with zinc for corrosion protection.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: C — Zinc**

### What galvanizing does
**Galvanizing**  is the process of applying a protective **zinc coating**  to iron or steel. In hot-dip galvanizing, suitably cleaned steel is immersed in molten zinc. The resulting coating includes bonded iron–zinc layers and an outer zinc-rich surface.

The coating protects the base metal in two related ways. First, it forms a physical barrier that reduces contact between steel and the surrounding moisture and oxygen. Second, zinc is electrochemically more active than iron and can corrode preferentially when both are exposed to an electrolyte. This is called sacrificial protection.

Sacrificial action explains why a small scratch need not immediately cause the exposed steel to rust as rapidly as unprotected steel. Protection is not unlimited: it depends on the surrounding coating remaining available and the exposure conditions. As the zinc is consumed, its protection eventually diminishes.

Galvanized steel is widely used for transmission-tower components, line hardware and conventional ACSR steel strands because these parts are exposed to the weather. The defining coating metal in the process is zinc.

### Quick Trick
G-alvanizing → Z-inc is the fixed pair to memorize.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A, B and D can be used in other coating/plating processes, but they are not the defining metal for galvanizing.

### Common Mistake
Confusing galvanizing with generic metal plating.
en.tip: Galvanizing = zinc; tinning = tin. Keep these two coating processes separate.

en.stem: Which one of the following is series unsymmetrical fault in power system?
en.quick: B — Open conductor fault. Breaking one or two phase conductors interrupts the series current path and creates an unbalanced three-phase condition.
formula: KEY CLASSIFICATION: Series fault → open conductor(s). Shunt faults → L-G, L-L, L-L-G, 3-phase faults.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: B — Open conductor fault**

### Series fault and phase imbalance
A **series fault**  changes or interrupts the normal path through which current flows along a conductor. When one phase conductor breaks, its series path becomes open. The other phase paths can remain connected, so the three phases no longer have identical circuit conditions. This makes an open-conductor fault an **unsymmetrical fault** .

For example, consider a three-phase feeder with one broken phase conductor. Current in the broken path is interrupted, while currents in the remaining phases depend on the load connection and available return paths. The voltage and current sets become unbalanced. An induction motor connected to such a supply may experience single-phasing, reduced torque and overheating.

This differs physically from a short circuit, which creates an unintended connection between phases or between a phase and earth. A series open circuit need not produce the very high current associated with a short circuit, so protection must also recognize conditions such as phase loss or negative-sequence current.

Opening one or two conductors produces unequal phase conditions. Simultaneously opening all three identical phase paths is a balanced interruption and is not the unsymmetrical case intended here.

### Quick Trick
Open = series; short = shunt.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A, C and D are classic unsymmetrical shunt faults. Only B represents a series interruption.

### Common Mistake
Calling every unsymmetrical fault a short-circuit fault.
en.tip: Fault classification shortcut: ‘open’ means series; ‘short’ means shunt.

subject: Electrical Engineering
concept: Operating Model of SVC versus STATCOM

en.stem: In Comparison between SVC and STATCOM which of the following statements is correct?
options: SVC has a larger dynamic range and STATCOM has a smaller dynamic voltage.
STATCOM acts as a voltage source behind a reactance and SVC acts as a variable susceptance.
SVC has faster response and better performance during transients and STATCOM has Somewhat slower response
STATCOM has higher generation of harmonics and SVC has lower generation of harmonics
en.quick: B — A STATCOM acts as a voltage source behind a reactance, while an SVC acts as a variable susceptance.
formula: ISTATCOM = (E − V)/(jX), for aligned voltage phasors
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: B — STATCOM acts as a voltage source behind a reactance and SVC acts as a variable susceptance.**

### SVC: variable shunt susceptance
A **Static Var Compensator (SVC)**  regulates reactive power using shunt capacitor and reactor branches controlled or switched by thyristors. Its fundamental-frequency equivalent is a controllable susceptance B connected to the bus. With capacitive injection defined as positive:

Q_SVC = V²B

At the limit of available capacitive susceptance, its maximum capacitive VAR output falls approximately with the square of bus voltage. This is an important limitation during a deep voltage reduction.

### STATCOM: controllable voltage behind reactance
A **STATCOM**  uses a voltage-source converter connected to the network through coupling reactance. If its converter voltage E is approximately in phase with bus voltage V, the voltage-magnitude difference drives reactive current:

I = (E − V)/(jX)

If E is greater than V, the STATCOM supplies capacitive reactive power to the bus. If E is smaller than V, it absorbs reactive power. The coupling reactance X limits and controls this current exchange.

A STATCOM can maintain approximately its rated reactive current over part of its low-voltage operating range, subject to converter limits. Its reactive power still decreases with voltage because Q is proportional to VI. The decisive distinction in this question is the equivalent model: **variable susceptance for SVC; voltage source behind reactance for STATCOM** .

### Quick Trick
SVC → B (susceptance); STATCOM → V-source.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A reverses the usual dynamic-performance comparison. C is incorrect because STATCOM is not the slower device. D is also opposite to the usual comparison; converter switching does create harmonics, but modern STATCOMs are not characterized simply as having ‘higher harmonics’ than SVCs as a defining advantage/disadvantage.

### Common Mistake
Assuming both devices are just variable capacitors. Their circuit models and low-voltage VAR characteristics are fundamentally different.
en.tip: Use the equivalent-circuit model to answer SVC-versus-STATCOM questions instead of memorizing isolated statements.

subject: Electrical Engineering
concept: Balanced Earth-Fault Protection for Small Generators

en.stem: Which protection is employed for generator rating from 1 MVA to 5 MVA?
en.quick: C — Balanced earth fault. This is the protection scheme associated with the 1–5 MVA generator range in the supplied paper.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: C — Balanced earth fault**

### How balanced earth-fault protection operates
**Balanced earth-fault protection**  detects earth faults inside a defined generator protection zone. In a typical arrangement, the residual current obtained from the three phase current transformers is compared with the current measured by a neutral current transformer. CT ratios, polarities and connections are selected so that the relay currents balance for healthy operation and faults outside the protected zone.

For normal balanced operation, the phasor sum of the three line currents is approximately zero. During an external earth fault, the corresponding phase-residual and neutral-current signals should balance at the relay. Little operating current therefore flows through its measuring element.

An earth fault within the CT-defined zone disturbs this balance. A difference or **spill current**  flows through the relay, which initiates tripping when its operating threshold is exceeded. The protected zone and sensitivity depend on the actual CT arrangement and generator neutral-earthing system.

The examination associates this relatively economical scheme with generators rated **1 MVA to 5 MVA** . The rating range is a textbook selection guide, not a universal design rule. Real generator protection is selected using winding arrangements, earthing, fault-current levels, required coverage and coordination.

### Quick Trick
Internal stator earth fault → look for a differential/balanced earth-fault scheme.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A is aimed at phase unbalance/negative-sequence conditions. B and D are time-graded overcurrent/earth-fault approaches and are less specifically matched to the keyed small-generator internal earth-fault scheme. C is the source-keyed scheme.

### Common Mistake
Assuming ‘balanced earth fault’ means the fault itself is balanced; the word refers to the protection scheme’s current balance.
en.tip: Generator protection questions often distinguish selective differential/earth-fault schemes from backup time-graded overcurrent schemes.

en.stem: The direction of induced e.m.f in a coil may be found with the help of:
en.quick: D — Fleming’s right-hand rule. For generator action, the thumb indicates motion, the first finger the magnetic field and the middle finger induced conventional current.
formula: Motional-EMF magnitude: e = Blv sin θ
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: D — Flemming’s Right hand rule**

### Applying Fleming’s right-hand rule
When a conductor moves across a magnetic field, charges in it experience a magnetic force. The resulting charge separation produces a **motional EMF** . Fleming’s right-hand rule relates the direction of conductor motion, magnetic field and induced EMF/current in generator action.

Hold the thumb, first finger and middle finger of the **right hand**  mutually perpendicular. Point the first finger in the magnetic-field direction, from north to south outside the magnet. Point the thumb in the direction of conductor motion. The middle finger then indicates the direction of induced conventional current if the circuit is closed.

For a rotating coil, apply the rule to each active conductor side using that side’s direction of motion and the local field direction. Their induced EMFs combine according to the coil connection. An open circuit can have induced EMF even though no sustained current flows.

For electromagnetic induction more generally, Lenz’s law determines the opposing sense of the induced effect, including cases with changing flux but no conductor motion. Faraday’s law, e = −N dΦ/dt, includes this opposition through its minus sign. The named hand rule expected by the paper is Fleming’s right-hand rule for generator action.

### Quick Trick
R = Right = induced EMF/generator.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A right-hand thumb rule is used for magnetic-field direction around a current-carrying conductor. B Faraday’s law primarily gives induced-EMF magnitude. C Fleming’s left-hand rule gives force/motion direction in motor action. D is the generator-direction rule.

### Common Mistake
Mixing Fleming’s right-hand and left-hand rules.
en.tip: Mnemonic: Generator gives electricity → Right hand; Motor produces motion → Left hand.

en.stem: Earthing of electrical equipment is necessary to prevent:
en.quick: C — Electric shock. Protective earthing bonds exposed conductive parts to a fault-current path and works with automatic disconnection to reduce shock risk.
formula: Touch voltage approximately: Vtouch = If × Zearth-path
Lower fault-path impedance → larger protective fault current → faster disconnection
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: C — Electric shock**

### What happens when insulation fails
The metal enclosure of electrical equipment is normally isolated from live conductors. If insulation fails and a live conductor touches the enclosure, the metal can become energized. A person touching it while in contact with earth or another conductive surface may then complete a dangerous current path.

**Protective earthing**  connects exposed conductive parts to the protective-conductor system. During a fault, this connection provides a designed path for fault current and helps limit hazardous potential differences. Suitable protective devices then disconnect the faulty circuit.

The exact disconnection mechanism depends on the earthing arrangement. A sufficiently low fault-loop impedance may allow a fuse or circuit breaker to operate promptly. In arrangements where earth-path impedance limits current, residual-current protection is particularly important. Earthing and the protective device must therefore work together.

Bonding also reduces differences of potential between simultaneously accessible conductive parts. Earthing does not guarantee that an equipment body stays at exactly zero volts during every fault, and it does not replace correct insulation or circuit protection. Its principal safety purpose in this question is to **prevent or reduce electric-shock danger from exposed metal becoming live** .

### Quick Trick
Equipment earthing → body protection from shock.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A harmonics require filtering/power-quality measures. B voltage fluctuations require regulation/system control. D overload is handled by overcurrent/thermal protection. C is the direct safety purpose of protective earthing.

### Common Mistake
Saying earthing prevents overload. It protects against dangerous exposed-conductive-part voltage during earth faults.
en.tip: Ask: ‘What happens if a live wire touches the metal body?’ Earthing provides the protective fault path.

en.stem: If two coils have self inductance L₁ and L₂ , then mutual inductance M between them is given by:
en.quick: C — M = k√(L₁L₂). The coupling coefficient k accounts for the fraction of magnetic coupling between the two coils.
formula: 0 ≤ k ≤ 1; M, L₁ and L₂ in H
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: C — M = k√(L₁L₂)**

### Relation between self and mutual inductance
**Self-inductance**  describes the flux linkage a coil produces in itself for a given current. **Mutual inductance**  describes the flux linkage produced in one coil by current in the other. Not all the flux generated by one coil necessarily links the second coil; some may follow leakage paths.

The coupling coefficient k expresses the degree of magnetic coupling. For the magnitude of mutual inductance in the usual passive two-coil model:

k = M/√(L₁L₂)

M = k√(L₁L₂), with 0 ≤ k ≤ 1

L₁, L₂ and M are measured in henrys, while k is dimensionless. When k = 0, the coils have no magnetic coupling. When k = 1, coupling is perfect and M reaches √(L₁L₂). Intermediate values represent partial coupling.

### Example of using the relation
If L₁ = 4 H, L₂ = 9 H and k = 0.5, first find the geometric mean of the two self-inductances, then apply the coupling factor:

√(L₁L₂) = √(4 × 9) = 6 H

M = 0.5 × 6 = 3 H

The induced voltage due to mutual coupling has magnitude M|di/dt|. Its polarity is determined by the dot convention and reference directions, rather than by changing the magnitude relation above.

### Quick Trick
M = k × geometric mean of L₁ and L₂.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A is dimensionally not generally correct. B puts k in the numerator of an inverse-inductance form and has wrong units. D is only true for perfect coupling k=1. C is the general relation.

### Common Mistake
Forgetting the coupling coefficient and choosing √(L₁L₂) for all coils.
en.tip: Use a units check: mutual inductance must be in henries.

en.stem: Case Study: An agricultural business purchased insurance coverage to protect against crop failure due to adverse weather conditions. What risk reduction approach did the business adopt?
en.quick: A — Risk transfer. Buying crop insurance shifts the covered financial consequences of crop failure to the insurer under the policy terms.
formula: KEY LOGIC: Insurance → contractual transfer of financial risk to an insurer.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: A — Risk transfer**

### Identifying the risk response in the case study
The agricultural business faces crop failure caused by adverse weather. The action described is the purchase of **insurance coverage** . Insurance creates a contract under which the business pays a premium and the insurer agrees to meet covered losses, subject to the policy conditions.

To classify this action, identify what has changed. The business still grows crops and remains exposed to adverse weather. Buying the policy does not itself prevent drought, heavy rainfall or crop damage. What changes is who bears the covered financial loss after the insured event occurs. This shift of financial responsibility is **risk transfer** .

For example, if a covered crop-loss claim is accepted, the insurer pays according to the agreed cover. The business may still retain a deductible, losses above the sum insured, excluded events or other uncovered expenses. Risk transfer can therefore be partial; it does not mean that every consequence of the event has disappeared.

In this question, the decisive evidence is the insurance contract. The premium is the cost of arranging the transfer, while the insurer’s obligation to compensate covered loss is the mechanism that makes it a risk-transfer response.

### Quick Trick
Insurance = transfer.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
B mitigation would reduce probability/impact through operational controls. C avoidance would stop the risky activity. D acceptance means retaining the loss exposure without transferring it. A matches insurance.

### Common Mistake
Calling insurance mitigation simply because it reduces financial pain. It transfers the covered financial consequence; it does not reduce the weather hazard itself.
en.tip: Classify the action, not the hazard: insurance changes who pays, so it is transfer.

subject: Electrical Engineering
concept: Reversing Phase Sequence by Interchanging Two Lines

en.stem: Phase sequence in three phase system can be reversed by:
options: Reversing the voltage polarity of all three phases
Reversing the voltage polarity of phase 1 and 2
Reversing the voltage polarity of phase 1
en.quick: A — Interchanging any pair of lines. Swapping two phase connections reverses their cyclic order and the direction of the rotating magnetic field.
formula: KEY LOGIC: ABC → interchange any two phases → ACB = reversed phase sequence.
After exchanging Y and B: R–B–Y
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: A — Interchanging any pair of lines.**

### Meaning of phase sequence
**Phase sequence**  is the order in which the three phase voltages reach corresponding points, such as their positive peaks. For a balanced R–Y–B system, the phase voltages are 120 electrical degrees apart, and their order repeats cyclically.

Interchange any two line connections while leaving the third unchanged. For example, exchanging Y and B changes R–Y–B into R–B–Y. The cyclic order is now reversed. The same reversal occurs when either of the other two pairs is interchanged.

Original sequence: R–Y–B

After exchanging Y and B: R–B–Y

In a three-phase motor, the time sequence of stator currents determines the direction of the rotating magnetic field. Reversing the phase sequence reverses this field direction and consequently changes the normal motor rotation direction.

A cyclic relabelling such as R–Y–B to Y–B–R does not reverse sequence; it merely changes the phase chosen as the starting reference. Similarly, shifting all three phase voltages by the same angle leaves their relative sequence unchanged. The required change is the **interchange of two lines** .

### Quick Trick
Any two phases → reverse rotation.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
B changes all phases together and does not create the required phase permutation. C and D describe polarity reversal rather than the standard method of changing phase sequence. A is the recognized method.

### Common Mistake
Thinking all three phases must be rearranged. Swapping just one pair is sufficient.
en.tip: Two lines swapped → sequence reversed; no calculation required.

en.stem: The steel used for transformer core has:
en.quick: D — High permeability. A high-permeability core provides a low-reluctance path and establishes the required flux with comparatively little magnetizing current.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: D — High permeability**

### Permeability and the magnetic circuit
A transformer core carries alternating magnetic flux linking the primary and secondary windings. The core material should have **high magnetic permeability** , so it offers a relatively easy path for this flux. In a simplified magnetic-circuit model:

Magnetic reluctance ℜ = l/(μA)

Φ = NI/ℜ

Here l is magnetic-path length, μ is permeability, A is core cross-sectional area and NI is magnetomotive force. Increasing μ reduces reluctance. For a specified flux, less magnetomotive force is then needed, so the magnetizing component of current is lower.

### Why this property matters in a transformer
Applied voltage and frequency largely determine the required alternating flux. High permeability allows that flux to be established without an unnecessarily large excitation current. Suitable electrical steel also has low hysteresis loss, while its silicon content increases electrical resistivity and thin insulated laminations restrict eddy currents.

Permeability should not be confused with retentivity, which describes the flux remaining after the magnetizing field is removed. Soft magnetic materials are often discussed using several related properties, but their remanence depends on the material and hysteresis loop. The supplied paper specifically keys **high permeability** . Near saturation, incremental permeability falls and excitation current rises sharply.

### Quick Trick
High μ → low magnetizing current.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A high hysteresis loss is undesirable. B low silicon content is not the desired design direction because silicon is used to improve magnetic/electrical loss properties. C low retentivity can be a desirable soft-magnetic property, making it a plausible distractor rather than a clearly wrong statement. D is the source-keyed and strongest canonical choice.

### Common Mistake
Treating a single textbook property as the only desirable magnetic property of a transformer core.
en.tip: Transformer core: high permeability + low hysteresis loss + high resistivity/low eddy-current loss.

en.stem:
Which of the following statements are correct about the Risk Benefit Analysis?
I. An approach to balance potential benefits against potential risks.
II. If the potential benefits outweigh the potential risks, the decision should proceed without any further evaluation.
III. It helps in making informed decisions by evaluating both risks and benefits.
IV. It helps in maximization of potential risks.
en.quick: B — Statements I and III only. Risk–benefit analysis compares potential benefits with risks to support an informed decision.
formula: KEY LOGIC: Risk–benefit analysis = structured comparison of expected benefits versus potential risks to support an informed decision.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: B — Statement I & III only correct**

### Evaluating the four statements
**Statement I is correct.**  Risk–benefit analysis compares the possible advantages of an action with its possible adverse consequences. This requires considering not only the size of outcomes but also their likelihood and uncertainty.

**Statement II is incorrect.**  A favourable initial comparison does not justify proceeding without any further evaluation. The decision may still require checking assumptions, assessing severe low-probability outcomes, choosing controls and examining the risk that remains after those controls.

**Statement III is correct.**  Examining both benefits and risks gives decision-makers a more complete basis for choosing between alternatives. It helps explain what can be gained, what can go wrong and what trade-offs are involved.

**Statement IV is incorrect.**  The aim is not to maximize potential risks. It is to make a justified decision about the benefits achievable and the level of risk that can be accepted or reduced.

The resulting sequence is **True, False, True, False** . Therefore, only Statements I and III are correct, which corresponds to **option B** . Risk–benefit analysis supports a reasoned decision; it does not automatically approve an action merely because an estimated benefit is larger than an estimated loss.

### Quick Trick
I = true, II = false, III = true, IV = false → I & III.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A includes false Statement II. C includes false Statements II and IV. D includes false Statement II. B contains the two correct statements I and III.

### Common Mistake
Assuming ‘benefits outweigh risks’ means no further controls, verification or evaluation are necessary.
en.tip: In multi-statement questions, mark T/F beside each statement first; then match the combination.

en.stem: At slack bus, which variables are specified ?
en.quick: A — Voltage magnitude |V| and phase angle δ. Slack-bus active and reactive power are calculated by the load-flow solution.
formula: Slack bus: specified |V| and δ; calculated P and Q
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: A — |V|, δ**

### Role of the slack bus in load flow
Each bus in an AC load-flow problem is described by four main quantities: active power P, reactive power Q, voltage magnitude |V| and voltage angle δ. Two are normally specified and the other two are determined. At the **slack bus** , also called the swing or reference bus, the specified quantities are **|V| and δ** .

The reference angle is commonly chosen as 0°. This establishes the angular reference for all other buses. Only differences in bus-voltage angles affect power flow, so one angle must be fixed to make the solution definite.

Network losses are not known accurately before the bus voltages and branch currents have been solved. The slack-bus power injection is allowed to adjust to the resulting mismatch between generation, demand and network losses. Thus P and Q at this bus are outputs of the conventional load-flow calculation.

For a system represented with one slack generator, its active-power contribution satisfies the system balance:

P_slack = ΣP_load + P_loss − ΣP_other generation

This is a mathematical role in the load-flow model. It does not mean that the physical generator has unlimited capability; its computed operating point must still satisfy equipment limits.

### Quick Trick
Slack sets the voltage reference: magnitude + angle.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
B P,Q describes a PQ/load bus. C |V|,P describes a PV/generator bus. D Q,δ is not the standard specified pair for a conventional load-flow bus type. A is correct.

### Common Mistake
Thinking the slack bus specifies P because it is a generator. Its P and Q are outputs of the load-flow solution.
en.tip: Bus classification is a high-yield memory table; learn both specified and calculated variables.

en.stem: Which color wire is used for earthing in India?
en.quick: D — Green. This is the traditional earthing-wire colour intended by the supplied options; modern protective-conductor identification commonly uses green-and-yellow.
formula: KEY RULE / STANDARD NOTE: Traditional exam convention → earth = green. Modern protective conductor identification → green/yellow combination under contemporary standards.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: D — Green**

### Identifying the protective conductor
The supplied paper identifies **green**  as the earthing-wire colour. This follows the traditional colour convention used in many Indian electrical-examination questions. Of the listed choices, green is the intended identification for the protective earthing conductor.

An earthing conductor connects exposed conductive equipment parts to the protective-conductor system. Its role is different from the neutral: the neutral can carry normal load-return or imbalance current, whereas the protective conductor serves the protective bonding and fault-current function.

Colour identification enables installers and maintenance personnel to distinguish these functions. In modern standardized wiring practice, the **green-and-yellow combination**  is widely used to identify protective conductors. Plain green in a historical multiple-choice question should therefore be understood in that examination context, rather than treated as a complete specification for every present-day installation.

For this PYQ, select **D — Green** , as marked in the source. For actual wiring, conductor identification must follow the applicable installation standard and documentation; colour alone is not proof that a conductor is safely connected or de-energized.

### Quick Trick
For this source PYQ: earth → green (D); modern practice → check green/yellow standard.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
Red, blue and black are not the intended earthing-conductor colour in the source convention. D is the only option representing the traditional earth colour.

### Common Mistake
Applying an old colour-code table to a modern installation without checking the current standard.
en.tip: Separate ‘exam-era convention’ from ‘current wiring standard’ when studying colour-code PYQs.

subject: Electrical Engineering
concept: Three-Phase Motor Current from Output Power and Efficiency

en.stem: A 50 kW, 400 V, 3 phase synchronous motor is operating at full load with an efficiency of 90%. If the field current is adjusted to make its power factor 0.8 leading, estimate the armature current.
en.quick: C — 100 A approximately. Electrical input is 50/0.90 = 55.56 kW, giving line current 55,555.56/(√3 × 400 × 0.8) = 100.23 A.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: C — 100 A**

### Given data and required current
The motor delivers **50 kW shaft output**  at full load. Its efficiency is 0.90, line voltage is 400 V, and power factor is 0.8 leading. The three-phase power equation uses electrical input power, so the shaft output must first be converted to input.

**Step 1: Calculate electrical input power.**  Efficiency is output power divided by input power:

η = P_out/P_in

P_in = 50,000/0.90 = 55,555.56 W

**Step 2: Write the balanced three-phase power equation.**  Using line voltage and line current:

P_in = √3 V_LI_Lcos φ

I_L = P_in/(√3 V_Lcos φ)

**Step 3: Substitute the values.**  Keep power in watts and voltage in volts to obtain amperes:

I_L = 55,555.56/(√3 × 400 × 0.8)

I_L = 100.23 A ≈ 100 A

Therefore, the matching answer is **C — 100 A** . A leading power factor means the current leads the voltage; it does not change the magnitude calculation because cos φ = 0.8.

The result is the **line current** , conventionally intended here by armature current. Winding phase current equals line current for star connection and line current divided by √3 for delta connection. The question gives no winding connection, so a separate phase-current value cannot be determined.

### Quick Trick
50/0.9≈55.6 kW; then divide by 1.732×400×0.8≈554 → about 100 A.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
138 A and 80 A do not satisfy the combined efficiency and three-phase power relation. 58 A is too low for 55.56 kW input at 400 V and 0.8 pf. C reproduces the rated output on back-substitution.

### Common Mistake
Using 50 kW directly as electrical input and ignoring 90% efficiency; that would under-estimate the current.
en.tip: Motor: P_in=P_out/η. Generator: P_out=ηP_in. Get this direction right before calculating current.

en.stem: Which of the following factor does not affect critical corona voltage while using bundled conductors?
en.quick: B — Length of line. Corona inception depends on the local conductor-surface electric field, not the total length of an otherwise identical uniform line.
formula: Corona inception depends on surface electric-field gradient
Typical form: Vd ∝ m₀ δ reff ln(Deff/reff)
Line length is not a local inception-voltage factor
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: B — Length of line**

### What determines corona inception
**Corona**  starts when the electric field at a conductor surface becomes strong enough to ionize the surrounding air. The critical corona voltage is therefore a field-threshold quantity. It depends on conductor geometry, spacing, surface condition and air conditions.

Bundling divides a phase conductor into several sub-conductors. The number of sub-conductors and their spacing change the distribution of charge and the maximum electric field at their surfaces. The distance between phase groups also affects the surrounding electric field. These geometric changes can therefore alter the corona-inception voltage.

### Why line length is the answer
Extending an otherwise identical, uniformly energized conductor increases how much conductor is present. It does not, by itself, change the local cross-sectional geometry or the critical surface field. Consequently, **total line length is not an independent local corona-inception parameter**  in the standard model used by this question.

Length can affect **total corona power loss** . If comparable corona loss occurs per kilometre, adding more kilometres increases the total loss. That is a different quantity from the voltage at which corona starts. Real lines can have nonuniform weather, voltage profiles and surface defects; the stated comparison assumes those local conditions are held constant.

The key distinction is therefore **inception voltage versus accumulated loss** . A simple single-conductor formula should not be treated as an exact bundled-conductor formula merely by replacing its radius with an equivalent bundle radius.

### Quick Trick
Critical voltage cares about geometry and air—not kilometres.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A, C and D affect bundle/conductor geometry and therefore surface gradient. B changes the amount of line but not the local critical field for otherwise identical geometry.

### Common Mistake
Choosing line length because total corona loss increases with length. The question asks critical voltage, not total loss.
en.tip: Corona inception = local electric-field problem; total loss = local loss × line length.

subject: Electrical Engineering
concept: Effect of Salt Content on Soil Resistivity

en.stem: What is the effect of present of salt on resistivity of soil?
options: Resistivity goes infinite with increase in salt content
Resistivity decreases with increase in salt content
Resistivity increases with increase in salt content
Resistivity remains constant with increase in salt content
en.quick: B — Resistivity decreases with increase in salt content. Dissolved salts add mobile ions to moist soil and increase its electrical conductivity.
formula: ρ in Ω·m; σ in S/m
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: B — Resistivity decreases with increase in salt content**

### Ionic conduction in soil
Electrical conduction through moist soil occurs largely through the water in the spaces between soil particles. Dissolved salts separate into positive and negative ions. Under an electric field, these ions move and carry current, increasing the conductivity of the pore water.

With adequate moisture and otherwise comparable conditions, increasing the concentration of dissolved salts generally increases soil conductivity σ. Resistivity ρ is its reciprocal:

ρ = 1/σ

A rise in conductivity therefore means a fall in resistivity. For example, if conductivity changes from 0.01 S/m to 0.02 S/m, the corresponding resistivity changes from 100 Ω·m to 50 Ω·m. This illustrates the inverse relation; it does not imply that doubling the salt content always doubles conductivity.

For the same electrode geometry, lower soil resistivity generally lowers earth-electrode resistance and improves current dissipation into the surrounding ground. The effect depends on the salt actually dissolving, so moisture and temperature also matter. Adding dry salt to very dry soil does not guarantee the same response.

The question asks for the physical trend, which is **decreasing resistivity with increasing dissolved salt content** . Practical soil-treatment decisions also consider corrosion and the long-term stability of the treatment.

### Quick Trick
Salt adds ions → resistance/resistivity falls.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A is physically opposite to ionic conduction. C predicts the wrong trend. D ignores the strong dependence of soil resistivity on moisture and dissolved salts. B is correct.

### Common Mistake
Confusing soil resistivity with corrosion rate; salts can lower resistivity while simultaneously increasing corrosion risk.
en.tip: Think conductivity first: more mobile ions → σ↑ → ρ↓.

en.stem: The lagging reactive power delivered by a line is proportional to ______ and is independent of ______.
en.quick: C — Line voltage drop; δ. This is the small-angle, predominantly reactive-line approximation; the exact reactive-power expression still contains cos δ.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: C — Line voltage drop; δ**

### Power flow through a lossless line
Consider a line represented by series reactance X, neglecting resistance and shunt charging. Let V_S and V_R be sending- and receiving-end voltage magnitudes, with angle difference δ. Using per-phase RMS quantities, the receiving-end powers are:

P_R = (V_SV_R/X) sin δ

Q_R = (V_SV_R cos δ − V_R²)/X

Positive Q_R represents lagging reactive power delivered at the receiving end. These equations show that active power depends strongly on angle, while reactive power depends strongly on voltage magnitude.

**Step 1: Apply the small-angle approximation.**  For small δ measured in radians, cos δ ≈ 1. Hence:

Q_R ≈ (V_SV_R − V_R²)/X

**Step 2: Factor out the receiving voltage.**  Define the voltage-magnitude drop as ΔV = V_S − V_R:

Q_R ≈ (V_R/X)(V_S − V_R)

Q_R ≈ (V_R/X)ΔV

At fixed V_R and X, lagging reactive power is approximately proportional to **voltage-magnitude drop** , and δ does not appear in this approximation. Thus option C is intended. The independence is not exact: at larger angles, the cos δ term matters, and resistance also couples voltage, angle, active power and reactive power.

### Quick Trick
Real power follows angle; reactive power follows voltage.

### Why Other Options Are Wrong
A reverses the dominant dependencies. B reactance affects the magnitude but reactive power is not independent of power angle in the exact expression simply as stated. D does not represent the standard decoupled relation. C matches the normal small-angle approximation.

### Common Mistake
Treating the ‘independent of δ’ statement as exact under all operating conditions; it is an approximation associated with a predominantly reactive line and small δ.
en.tip: P–δ and Q–V is one of the most useful power-system approximation pairs.

subject: Electrical Engineering
concept: System Benefits of Power Factor Improvement

en.stem: What is the significance of power factor improvement in power systems?
options: It helps to create transients in the power system.
It decreases the overall power generation capacity.
It helps to increase the cost of transmission lines.
It minimizes the reactive power burden on generators and transmission equipment.
en.quick: D — It minimizes the reactive power burden on generators and transmission equipment. Local compensation reduces the reactive current carried upstream.
en.detailed:
**Correct answer: D — It minimizes the reactive power burden on generators and transmission equipment.**

### Why low power factor burdens the network
An inductive load draws active power P to perform useful work and reactive power Q to maintain its electromagnetic fields. The supply equipment must carry the resulting apparent power S, even though reactive power does not represent net energy converted into useful work over a full AC cycle.

S = √(P² + Q²)

Power factor = P/S

Power-factor improvement supplies part of the reactive requirement locally, for example through a capacitor bank. This reduces the net reactive power demanded from the upstream network while the useful active-power requirement can remain unchanged.

### Effect on current and equipment capacity
I_L = P/(√3 V_Lcos φ)

At fixed active power and voltage, a higher power factor means a smaller line current. The lower current reduces I²R losses, reduces the current-related voltage drop and releases some of the kVA capacity of generators, transformers and lines.
